explain.say: Seawater has about 35 grams of salt in every litre, far too much to drink. Reverse osmosis plants push the water through a special membrane to separate it from the salt.

faq.a: Osmosis is when water naturally moves through a membrane towards the saltier side. Reverse osmosis pushes hard enough to force water the opposite way, out of the salty side, leaving the salt behind.
asks: How do you take the salt out of seawater?
What does a desalination membrane do?

faq.a: Forcing water through the membrane needs very high pressure, which takes a lot of electricity for the pumps. Many plants recover energy from the high-pressure brine to cut costs.
asks: How much energy does desalination use?

faq.a: It stays in the leftover water, called brine, which is about twice as salty as the sea. It is piped back to the sea and mixed carefully so it does not harm sea life.
Boiling and condensing the steam works, and some plants do it, but it takes even more energy than reverse osmosis in most places.
Dry countries such as Saudi Arabia, Israel and the United Arab Emirates get much of their drinking water from desalination plants on their coasts.

facts: Seawater contains on average about 35 grams of dissolved salt per litre.
Seawater reverse osmosis plants typically operate at pressures of about 55 to 80 bar.

quiz.say: In reverse osmosis, what is forced through the membrane?
quiz.show: In reverse osmosis, what is forced through the membrane?
quiz.why: The membrane lets water molecules through but holds back the dissolved salt.

wrong.1: Salt is held back by the membrane; that is the whole point.
wrong.2: Sand is removed by the pre-filters before the membrane.
